hook: SCP-INTEGER is a file written under its own rules: the anomaly reacts to being named the wrong way, so the document talks about itself almost entirely in capitalised stand-in words like THING, HAZARD and FILE. The first screen or two will look baffling. Treat the vocabulary as part of the puzzle and keep going; the interview in the middle is where the mechanics click.
whyItMatters: The danger here lives in language and paperwork rather than in a physical object, which the opening notice from the Department of Miscommunications frames as a semiohazard: a fact that shouldn't be true but works anyway. The esoteric-class label and the colour-coded identifiers signal that the article is playing with the format itself. It works as comedy as much as puzzle, with a running gag built around the Site Director's name.
thingsToNotice:
The whole mechanism is retroactive. Any wrong name for the anomaly is pushed one step more abstract and written into the list of 'correct' names as if it had always been there, and whatever carried the slip, a page, a recorder, a person, becomes an instance too. That is why the Site-15 Director is stuck with names like Placeholder McDoctorate, PhD.: he was the first instance, after speaking the thing's true name, and the result is legally his name.

In the interview the questioner casually calls the situation an issue, a breeze passes through the room, and ISSUE is suddenly on the identifier list. He then realises he has always been INQUISITOR and SCIENTIST-LETTER, and the Director finally understands why he has been calling him that for years; the amnestic he asks for afterwards is not expected to help. The pop-up footnotes (a mortal speaking a true name, PUNISHMENT, a restricted FORBIDDEN entry) hint at a mythic layer, and the closing parable makes it explicit by recasting the anomaly as a sentence passed on anyone who names what ought not to be named.
